stories.headline: Will back all meaningful efforts for Ukraine peace, PM Modi assures Poland's Tusk
stories.title: Will back all meaningful efforts for Ukraine peace, PM Modi assures Poland's Tusk
stories.summary: PM Modi and his Polish counterpart Tusk expressed deepest concern in a joint statement over the war in Ukraine, including its tragic humanitarian consequences and the impact on Global South. In his media statement, Modi assured Tusk that whether it is Ukraine or West Asia, India will continue to support every meaningful effort for peace.

stories.headline: Cryosphere-related Hazards in the Himalaya
stories.title: Cryosphere-related Hazards in the Himalaya
stories.summary: The Himalaya is undergoing profound environmental transformation. Rising temperatures, retreating glaciers, degrading permafrost and changing precipitation patterns are reshaping mountain landscapes and increasing the potential for cascading hazards. Rock and ice avalanches, glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), glacier detachments and extreme floods are no longer distant possibilities. They are immediate concerns for mountain communities, infrastructure planners and disaster management authorities. The catastrophic rock and ice avalanche at Chamoli, Uttarakhand, in February 2021 involved approximately 26 million m³ of material, comprising nearly 80% rock and 20% glacier ice, with the detached mass reaching a thickness of about 180 m. The collapse transformed into a destructive debris flow that swept through downstream valleys, destroying the Rishiganga hydropower project and severely damaging the Tapovan Vishnugad project, while claiming more than 200 lives or leaving people missing. A similar but much larger disaster struck the Rasuwa region of Nepal on 26 August 2026, when a rock and ice avalanche, preliminarily estimated at around 100 million m³, triggered a devastating flood that travelled more than 180 km downstream. The disaster affected 12 hydropower projects and resulted in at least 1,455 reported deaths, with hundreds more people missing in the aftermath. Originating near the Nepal-China border, the event also highlights the transboundary dimensions of mountain hazards, with consequences extending across interconnected river systems and infrastructure networks. Together, these disasters underscore the capacity of high mountain mass movements to trigger cascading impacts far downstream, often leaving communities and infrastructure with little time to respond. The October 2023 South Lhonak glacial lake outburst flood in Sikkim exposed the cascading risks associated with rapidly changing cryospheric environments. The disaster involved a permafrost slope failure estimated at approximately 14 million m³, triggering a flood wave that displaced around 50 million m³ of water, while an estimated 270 million m³ of material was eroded along the channel. The resulting deluge devastated the Teesta River valley, destroyed the Teesta III hydropower project, and severely affected infrastructure and settlements along a 64 km stretch downstream, claiming more than 170 lives. Beyond its immediate impacts in India, the event underscored the transboundary implications of cryosphere-related hazards for downstream communities in Bangladesh. Such disasters demonstrate that hazards originating in remote glacial catchments can propagate across extensive river networks, threatening communities, infrastructure and livelihoods far beyond their source areas. In the Union Territory of Ladakh, the Gya GLOF of 2014 and other events highlight the vulnerability of mountain communities to sudden flood events. In this cold, arid region, streams are lifelines, sustaining villages, irrigation, and livelihoods. Their sudden transformation into destructive flood corridors can devastate agricultural land, damage infrastructure, and disrupt communities. Jammu and Kashmir faces its own set of cryosphere-related risks. Our recent study published in the Journal of Glaciology assessed 155 glacial lakes across the Kashmir Himalaya using satellite observations from 1992 to 2024. We documented a 26% increase in the area of ice contact proglacial lakes, while five lakes were classified as having very high GLOF susceptibility. The potential exposure includes thousands of buildings, 15 major bridges, roads, and a hydropower project. For Kashmir, these findings are a call for action. Potentially hazardous lakes and their downstream corridors must be identified, vulnerable settlements and infrastructure assessed, and early warning and evacuation systems strengthened. Scientific assessments must inform land use planning and infrastructure development before a disaster strikes, rather than being revisited only after lives and livelihoods have been lost. Hydropower development across the Himalaya, particularly along the Chenab River, warrants careful, science-based scrutiny. Small glacial lake outburst floods have also been documented in the Chenab basin, fortunately without reported impacts on hydropower infrastructure. However, the possibility of future events of substantially greater magnitude, potentially triggering cascading hazards, cannot be ruled out. Hydropower remains important for regional development and energy security, but powerhouses, access roads, tunnels and associated infrastructure must be planned with due consideration of upstream cryospheric hazards, unstable slopes, flood pathways and cascading impacts. Conventional engineering assessments alone may not adequately capture risks originating far upstream or evolving under a changing climate. Infrastructure resilience, therefore, requires integrated catchment-scale hazard assessments, scenario-based modelling and continuous monitoring for risk mitigation in increasingly dynamic mountain environments. The way forward requires a shift from reactive disaster management to anticipatory risk reduction. First, potentially hazardous glacial lakes, unstable slopes and vulnerable stream corridors must be systematically identified through satellite remote sensing, geophysical investigations and hydrodynamic modelling. Second, early warning systems must combine real-time lake and river monitoring, rainfall and seismic observations, reliable communication networks and community-based evacuation protocols. A warning system is effective only when the warning reaches people in time, and they know what to do. Third, development must respect the physical geography of mountain valleys. Based on recent experiences, a precautionary buffer of at least 300 meters along identified high-hazard stream corridors should be considered for restricting new infrastructure, subject to detailed geomorphological and flood modelling. This should not be interpreted as a universally safe or sufficient distance; actual exclusion zones must reflect the terrain and potential inundation extent. Ecozonation plans should guide settlements, roads, hydropower projects and tourism infrastructure away from high hazard areas. The use of geospatial artificial intelligence offers a powerful approach utilizing big data for detecting changes in glacial lakes, mapping unstable terrain, identifying exposed infrastructure and supporting scenario-based planning. However, these technologies must complement, not replace, field observations, engineering assessments and local knowledge. The message for this International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction is clear. These disasters are neither the first nor, certainly, the last. We cannot prevent every avalanche or outburst flood, but we can prevent avoidable exposure and reduce the loss of lives and livelihoods. The Himalaya needs development that respects its changing environment, informed by science, guided by precaution and centered on the safety of its people. Dr. Irfan Rashid is Associate Professor and Head, Department of Geoinformatics at the University of Kashmir. His research focuses on cryospheric processes, mountain hazards, and climate change in the Himalaya.

stories.headline: The Cage, the Keys, and the Command
stories.title: The Cage, the Keys, and the Command
stories.summary: Two years into Omar Abdullah’s government, its critics have chosen familiar trenches. One side lists broken promises, the other revisits the National Conference’s old sins. Both are partisan. Neither is a ledger. A fair ledger asks three questions of every promise. Was it within his authority? If not, what did he do about it? If it was, why is there a gap? A commander answers for what lies within his command, and for what he does about the rest. Applied honestly, the test clears Omar Abdullah of some charges and convicts him of others. The government has been honest about the cage, but not yet about the unlocked doors. Statehood, Article 370, the Public Safety Act, police and public order are not in the Chief Minister’s gift. Grading him on them grades the wrong man. A July 2024 amendment strengthened the Lieutenant Governor’s hold over police, public order, All India Services officers and prosecution sanctions. The cabinet’s business rules, approved in March 2025, remain unsettled after the LG returned them with queries. In April 2025, the LG transferred 48 JKAS officers while those rules were pending. Omar has said that SKIMS, the universities and the Power Development Corporation now sit with the unelected side. The purse is no freer. Of the ₹1.27 lakh crore budget for 2026–27, only about ₹31,800 crore is expected from the government’s own resources. Of ₹90,018 crore in projected revenue receipts, ₹58,218 crore, about 65 per cent, is expected as central grants. On statehood, the Centre has offered no timeframe. Omar has met Amit Shah five times and been told, in effect, “at an appropriate time.” He has said the PSA will go by ordinance the day full powers return. A Union Territory assembly cannot legislate on police or public order at all. A BJP spokesman has demanded a two-year report card. The largest unmet promise on that card is one only the BJP’s government can keep. Yet where authority lies with the elected government, the record is more mixed. Power, recruitment, daily-wage regularisation and targeted welfare show delay, dilution or incomplete delivery. Omar holds the Power and Finance portfolios himself. From 1 September 2026, electricity tariffs rose by an average of 6.83 per cent, even as Kashmir faces a winter shortfall of roughly 800 MW. The promised 200 free units were narrowed to Antyodaya households, about 2.23 lakh families. The Centre cleared the scheme in February 2026; by September, vendors were still being evaluated. On jobs, the manifesto promised vacancies filled within 180 days. JKPSC advertised 357 posts in 2025–26 against 2,586 in 2023–24; JKSSB advertised 1,731 against 5,044 in 2024–25. Advertised posts are not appointments, and the earlier figures largely belong to the LG’s administration. Even so, the direction is wrong, and the 180-day promise remains distant. Daily wagers are the starkest case. A committee under the Chief Secretary was formed in March 2025 with six months to report. Its report has not been tabled, and estimates of the workforce range from over 50,000 to over a lakh. Whatever needs the LG’s signature, this file has not yet reached his desk. LPG relief has shrunk from twelve free cylinders to six, for Antyodaya households only, and there is no sign of the promised ₹5,000 a month for women who head poor households. The ledger, however, is not blank. His March 2025 budget was the first presented by an elected government in seven years, and the 2026–27 budget followed on schedule. Free bus travel for women began within months of the promise. Marriage assistance for girls from Antyodaya households rose from ₹50,000 to ₹75,000. The Darbar Move was restored. Mission YUVA shows activity. By 31 August 2026, it had received 1,00,407 applications and disbursed 32,156 loans. Those are loans, not jobs. The scheme is a real administrative achievement, but not yet an employment outcome. Its success must be judged by enterprise survival and hiring, not disbursement alone. The railway link to Kashmir was begun decades before this government took office. Its completion falls in this tenure, but the credit does not. Zuhaib Yusuf Mir’s charge of “surrender” is rhetoric. The government passed two Assembly resolutions and, in July, took its demand to Delhi, where police stopped the Chief Minister short of the protest venue. But his question about sequencing deserves an answer. Omar gave the Centre nearly two years of quiet talks before announcing the “Delhi Chalo” campaign. The September 2026 resolution sought full statehood alone, and he urged his members not to press amendments on special status. That was tactically defensible, since it denied the BJP an easy pretext. But it also confirmed a strategic retreat, from restoration of special status and autonomy to the narrower demand for statehood. The electorate has noticed. The National Conference lost Budgam, its first defeat there since 1977, while its own MP, Aga Ruhullah Mehdi, stayed out of the campaign. Patience with New Delhi has bought no timeline, and dissent at home is growing. The ledger must also be regional. A government elected across Jammu and Kashmir cannot measure itself only by Srinagar’s political anxieties or the Valley’s grievances. Jammu’s voters will ask whether power supply, recruitment, daily-wage regularisation and development funds have reached their districts with the same urgency. The Darbar Move may have been restored, but restoration of a ritual is not restoration of regional confidence. If Delhi has clipped the government’s wings, it must still explain why the powers it possesses have not been used with equal energy in Jammu, Chenab Valley, Pir Panjal and the Kashmir Valley alike. Sunil Sethi’s history of the National Conference and the Congress is a debate for another day. It does not tell a daily wager, twenty years in service, whether his file is moving. Nor does it excuse a Centre that holds the key to statehood. The government has three years left. It should publish a public scorecard: every manifesto promise, the department responsible, the order or budget line behind it, the number of beneficiaries and the date. Where the LG or Centre holds the key, the scorecard should say so. Where Omar holds it, it should say that too. This would answer critics better than another resolution and oblige adversaries to argue facts. Delhi holds the key to statehood. Omar holds the keys to recruitment, power, welfare and the daily wager’s file. He may blame the cage. He cannot blame every unlocked door. Responsibility without authority is an injustice; authority without accountability is negligence. This government may protest the first, but it must answer for the second. (The writer is a former Indian Army officer. He writes on issues pertaining to Jammu & Kashmir)

stories.headline: Will decide on any notice to remove CEC according to rules: LS Speaker Om Birla
stories.title: Will decide on any notice to remove CEC according to rules: LS Speaker Om Birla
stories.summary: Both the Lok Sabha Speaker and the Rajya Sabha chairman had rejected previous notices from the opposition, saying their allegations “do not prima facie meet the high constitutional bar for removal proceedings”. Birla noted the process for removal of the chief election commissioner was the same as for removing a Supreme Court judge.
